name: point versus displacement vector
essential_semantics: Points and vectors are different types: point minus point is a vector, point plus vector is a point, point plus point is meaningless.
canonical_example: P - Q is a displacement; P + Q is not defined
rationale: The affine/linear distinction is the geometric analogue of the interval/ratio scale distinction and prevents a real class of errors.

name: affine space and affine combinations
essential_semantics: A space acted on freely and transitively by a vector space, where only weight-one combinations of points are defined.
canonical_example: the midpoint (P + Q)/2 is affine; P + Q is not
rationale: Convex combinations are affine combinations with non-negative weights; the affine structure is what makes them legitimate.

name: Euclidean space with dimension
essential_semantics: R^n with the standard inner product, where the dimension is part of the type.
canonical_example: x in R^3
rationale: The default ambient space for applied geometry and multivariate analysis; dimension mismatch is a checkable error.

name: distance with an identified metric
essential_semantics: Which metric is being used (Euclidean, Manhattan, geodesic, Mahalanobis) is part of the statement.
canonical_example: Mahalanobis distance uses Sigma^{-1}
rationale: Unqualified 'distance' is ambiguous and the choice changes results; it also carries units.

name: angle with units and range convention
essential_semantics: Angles as dimensionless-but-unit-bearing quantities with radian/degree distinguished and the principal range stated.
canonical_example: atan2 returns an angle in (-pi, pi]
rationale: Degree/radian confusion is a classic real-world failure, and angle is the canonical dimensionless-with-unit case.

name: topological space
essential_semantics: A set with a declared topology, so that continuity and convergence are relative to a named structure.
canonical_example: (X, tau) with tau a collection of open sets
rationale: Topology is the minimal structure for continuity; assuming the standard topology on R^n is an unrecorded commitment.

name: open, closed, interior, closure, boundary
essential_semantics: These are properties relative to an ambient space, and open and closed are not complementary properties of sets.
canonical_example: [0,1) is neither open nor closed in R
rationale: Whether a feasible set is closed determines whether an optimum is attained; a real practical consequence.

name: compactness
essential_semantics: Every open cover has a finite subcover, with the Heine-Borel characterisation valid only in specific settings.
canonical_example: a continuous function on a compact set attains its maximum
rationale: Existence of extrema is a compactness theorem; asserting attainment without it is unjustified.

name: connectedness and path-connectedness
essential_semantics: Distinct notions with an implication in only one direction, both relative to a topology.
canonical_example: the intermediate value theorem needs connectedness of the domain
rationale: Domain connectivity is a hypothesis in several standard theorems and is often assumed silently for piecewise domains.

name: continuous map between spaces
essential_semantics: Preimages of open sets are open; continuity is relative to the topologies on both source and target.
canonical_example: f : (X, tau_X) -> (Y, tau_Y) continuous
rationale: It generalises analytic continuity and parallels measurability, both of which are two-structure relations.

name: homeomorphism and topological invariants
essential_semantics: Bicontinuous bijection; invariants are properties preserved by it.
canonical_example: a circle and a square are homeomorphic
rationale: The topological analogue of isomorphism, useful for testing whether structural equivalence is representable.

name: homotopy and deformation
essential_semantics: Continuous deformation between maps, generating invariants such as the fundamental group.
canonical_example: a loop in the punctured plane has a winding number
rationale: Included to mark the far end of topological expressiveness rather than as an expected capability.

name: manifold with dimension and smoothness
essential_semantics: A space locally homeomorphic to R^n with a declared dimension and smoothness class.
canonical_example: the sphere S^2 as a 2-dimensional smooth manifold
rationale: Constraint surfaces and parameter spaces with structure (simplex, positive-definite cone) are manifolds.

name: charts, atlases and coordinate patches
essential_semantics: Local coordinates valid on a patch, with transition maps on overlaps; no global coordinates assumed.
canonical_example: latitude-longitude fails at the poles
rationale: Local-only validity is a general and underappreciated pattern that a representation should be able to record.

name: tangent space at a point
essential_semantics: A vector space attached to each point, where the base point is part of the vector's identity.
canonical_example: v in T_p M
rationale: Gradients on constrained spaces live in tangent spaces; ignoring the base point produces invalid updates.

name: vector field
essential_semantics: An assignment of a tangent vector to each point, with divergence and curl as derived operations.
canonical_example: the velocity field of a fluid
rationale: Physical fields are point-indexed vectors with units; representing them as arrays loses both.

name: differential forms and orientation
essential_semantics: Antisymmetric multilinear objects integrated over oriented submanifolds, with exterior derivative.
canonical_example: Stokes theorem: integral of d omega over M equals integral of omega over the boundary
rationale: It is the correct type of an integrand on a manifold, distinct from a scalar function.

name: metric tensor and induced geometry
essential_semantics: A field of inner products determining lengths, angles and volumes, possibly non-Euclidean.
canonical_example: the Fisher information metric on a statistical manifold
rationale: Information geometry and relativity both need a non-flat metric; assuming Euclidean geometry is a modelling commitment.

name: curvature
essential_semantics: Local deviation from flatness, derived from the metric, with the specific curvature notion identified.
canonical_example: Gaussian curvature of a sphere is 1/r^2
rationale: Included to bound the geometric end of the ontology; low expectation for a general mathematical IR.

name: geodesic and shortest path
essential_semantics: Locally length-minimising curve determined by the metric, whose existence and uniqueness are conditional.
canonical_example: great circles on a sphere
rationale: A variational problem on a manifold, combining several capabilities at once.

name: group of transformations and invariance
essential_semantics: Rotations, translations, similarities acting on a space, with invariance of a quantity as a statable property.
canonical_example: the Euclidean distance is invariant under rigid motions
rationale: Invariance claims are a major class of mathematical statement and require the group to be nameable.

name: named coordinate system
essential_semantics: Cartesian, polar, spherical, cylindrical with the convention (angle order, sign) explicit and the validity region stated.
canonical_example: (r, theta) with r >= 0 and theta in [0, 2 pi)
rationale: Coordinate conventions differ between fields and change integration measures; leaving them implicit is lossy.

name: change of coordinates with Jacobian factor
essential_semantics: Transformation between coordinate systems including the volume-element correction.
canonical_example: dA = r dr dtheta in polar coordinates
rationale: Forgetting the Jacobian factor is a canonical silent error shared by geometry and probability.

name: convex set
essential_semantics: Closed under convex combinations, with convexity as a checkable property of a described set.
canonical_example: {x : Ax <= b} is convex
rationale: Convexity of the feasible set is the property that makes optimisation tractable and local optima global.

name: polyhedra and polytopes
essential_semantics: Intersections of half-spaces with vertex and facet descriptions as alternative views of one object.
canonical_example: the feasible region of a linear program
rationale: H-representation and V-representation are two faithful views of one object, a good multi-view test.

name: probability simplex as a constrained domain
essential_semantics: Non-negative vectors summing to one, a constrained manifold that is not an open subset of R^n.
canonical_example: p in Delta^{k-1}: p_i >= 0, sum p_i = 1
rationale: Categorical parameters live on the simplex; treating them as free vectors produces invalid gradients and invalid samples.

name: cones and generalised inequalities
essential_semantics: A closed convex cone inducing a partial order, such as the PSD cone with the Loewner order.
canonical_example: A preceq B means B - A is positive semidefinite
rationale: Matrix inequalities are cone inequalities, not elementwise ones; conflating them is a real modelling error.

name: projection onto a set or subspace
essential_semantics: Nearest-point map relative to a metric, with existence and uniqueness requiring convexity and closedness.
canonical_example: least-squares fit projects y onto the column space of X
rationale: Least squares is a projection statement; the geometric view carries the orthogonality condition explicitly.

name: volume, area and surface measures
essential_semantics: Measures induced by the geometry, with dimension-dependent units and the correct measure for a submanifold.
canonical_example: surface area measure on the sphere
rationale: Uniform distributions on geometric domains require the right base measure; getting it wrong changes the distribution.

name: orientation and handedness
essential_semantics: A choice of sign convention for ordered bases or boundaries, preserved through transformations.
canonical_example: a right-handed coordinate frame
rationale: Sign conventions in physics and graphics are orientation choices that must survive translation between systems.
